summary: State e4078c2b5177a1ac (source level) is 1.887x faster than amdclang's build (240 pairs, CI 1.883 to 1.892; 0.0846 ms against 0.1598 ms), static check and the full 49-case battery pass. It launches one 64-lane wave per output instead of a 256-thread workgroup: each lane reads 4 consecutive floats with one global_load_dwordx4 (per-element guarded loads only in the tail block), sums them, and the wave reduces with the shuffle chain; there is no LDS, no barrier and no second reduction stage. Results match within the manifest tolerance, not bit for bit (the summation order changed). Case: the reference was not memory-bound (reference headroom 2.45, every element read once); the winning state sits at headroom 1.30 (3.2 TB/s), and nothing tried closed the rest.

DPP syntax and the wave-reduce idiom (4 DPP adds per row, v_readlane at lanes 0/16/32/48) are not in the agc skill; I found them by grepping agc/gen/rowwise.py. A `wave_reduce` transform or a snippet in the skill would help.

probe was not needed here, but there is no tool that separates wave-launch cost from memory time: the best state is at headroom 1.30 and I could not tell whether the remaining 20 us is dispatch of 262144 waves or the read rate; a 'loads only' or 'empty waves on the same grid' diagnostic would answer it.

source(): sweeping EPL needs the whole source text resent even with defines, because the launch grid expression changes with the define; launch expressions that can reference the defines would make the sweep one-liners.
bench/llm/sessions/ had no recipes on disk (Glob found none) although the notes point there.
lessons: Block reductions written as 'one element per thread + warp reduce + LDS + barrier + second warp reduce' (MIOpen block_reduce, 256 threads per output) are far from the memory floor (headroom 2.45, 1.68 TB/s). One wave per output with 4 floats per lane (global_load_dwordx4) and a single in-wave reduction gave 1.89x and 3.2 TB/s; this is a source-level rewrite of about 25 lines.

For that structure, 4 floats per lane (1 KB per wave) beat 8 per lane (1.83x) and 16 per lane (1.81x); block 64 and block 256 are equal within noise (1.887 vs 1.878). Consistent with the note that many short waves touching about 1 KB each are what the memory system likes.

Replacing amdclang's 6-step ds_bpermute shuffle chain (6 lgkmcnt waits, per-lane 64-bit address math and guards) with scalar addressing, 4 DPP adds and 4 v_readlane in a hand-written fast path changed nothing (1.854 vs 1.887, overlapping CIs): once a wave issues one x4 load and stores one float, its ALU and bpermute work is not on the critical path.
coarsen on a loop-free one-load-per-wave state does not pay: factor 2 is 0.99x of the parent, factor 4 is 0.93x.

Tails: guarding with 'if (base + EPL <= N) wide load else per-element guarded loads' compiles to an exec-masked x4 path plus a rarely taken per-element path, passed all shape variants (N = 1, 10000 to 10008) and costs nothing measurable.

session.final:
`mo_reduce_sum` now runs **1.89x faster** than amdclang's build (0.0846 ms against 0.1598 ms; 240 pairs, CI 1.883 to 1.892). The state to ship is `e4078c2b5177a1ac`; it passes the static check and the full 49-case battery, and the report is filed.

- **What changed:** one 64-lane wave per output instead of a 256-thread workgroup. Each lane reads 4 consecutive floats in one wide load and the wave reduces in place, with no LDS, no barrier and no second reduction stage. The last, partial block falls back to per-element guarded loads.
- **Rounding:** results match within the manifest tolerance, not bit for bit, because the summation order changed.
- **Which case this is:** the baseline was not memory-bound (reference headroom 2.45, every element read once). The winning state sits at headroom 1.30 (about 3.2 TB/s), and nothing I tried closed the rest.

Everything else tried on top of the winner was equal or slower:

| Variant | State | Speedup vs amdclang |
|---|---|---|
| 4 floats per lane, block 64 (shipped) | `e4078c2b5177a1ac` | 1.887 |
| Same code, block 256 | `7e423b92a66d2d69` | 1.878 |
| 8 floats per lane | `a7cd4477b6b7716f` | 1.829 |
| 16 floats per lane | `9bdfee69b33a764d` | 1.810 |
| Hand-written fast path with DPP reduction | `e9a0f92d90fceb24` | 1.854 |
| `coarsen` factor 2 | `3c6e825c594ec515` | 1.869 |
| `coarsen` factor 4 | `01f3f9af33d17df4` | 1.760 |

I stopped after seven timed candidates, well short of the budget, because three different kinds of follow-up (wider lanes, cheaper reduction, coarsening) each brought nothing. I could not tell whether the remaining 20 us or so is wave dispatch or read rate; that is listed in the friction notes.
